title: A Quantity Takeoff, From First Principles
summary: A concrete floor breaks down into three quantities: concrete volume, reinforcement weight and formwork contact area. The concrete is easy to check, but the formwork carries the labour that sets the floor cycle, so that is where the owner looks hardest.
body:
Mr Shabazz, a quantity takeoff turns a drawing into numbers you can price and check. Check the concrete because it is easy to verify; interrogate the formwork because that is where the money and the schedule are.

In plain English

Every price for building work is a quantity multiplied by a rate. The quantity comes from the drawings; the rate comes from the market and the contractor's methods. An owner cannot usually judge rates without local data, but he can check quantities himself in minutes, and doing so anchors every conversation that follows. A bidder who cannot or will not show his quantities is telling you something about his price.

The three quantities in a concrete floor

Concrete volume is length times width times thickness, plus a waste allowance for spillage, over-depth and pump line losses. It drives the order, the number of trucks and the length of pour day.

Reinforcement is designed by the engineer bar by bar, but at planning stage it is estimated from a ratio: kilograms of steel per cubic metre of concrete, plus an allowance for laps where bars overlap. The ratio varies widely with the structural system and the loads, so it is a rule of thumb, not a design figure. The better comparison across bids is kilograms of steel per square metre of floor, because it removes the effect of slab thickness.

Formwork is measured as contact area: the area of mould that touches the concrete. For a flat slab that is the soffit, the underside, plus the edges. Formwork is mostly labour, it is reused floor after floor, and the speed at which a crew can strike, move and re-erect it sets the floor cycle, the number of days per floor. That cycle drives the whole frame programme.

A worked example

Take a hypothetical flat slab 30 metres by 20 metres, 0.25 metres thick, with a plan perimeter of 100 metres.

  1. Concrete: 30 times 20 times 0.25 equals 150 cubic metres. Add 5 percent waste, 7.5 cubic metres, for 157.5, ordered as 158 cubic metres. At 8 cubic metres a truck that is 20 loads.
  2. Reinforcement at a planning ratio of 100 kilograms per cubic metre: 150 times 100 equals 15,000 kilograms. Add 10 percent for laps: 16,500 kilograms, or 16.5 tonnes.
  3. Normalise it: the floor area is 600 square metres, so 16,500 divided by 600 is 27.5 kilograms per square metre. If one bidder carries 22 and another 34 for the same floor, one of them has misread the drawings or knows something the other does not.
  4. Formwork: soffit 600 square metres, plus edges of 100 metres times 0.25 metres, 25 square metres, for 625 square metres of contact area.
  5. Time: suppose a crew erects 120 square metres of soffit formwork a day. 600 divided by 120 is 5 days, plus reinforcement, services and the pour, so perhaps a 7-day floor cycle. If the bid assumes 6 days and the crew achieves 8, each floor costs two extra days, and across eight floors that is 16 working days of preliminaries the contractor did not price.

Rates and the price

Multiply each quantity by a local rate and you have the direct cost of the floor. Hypothetically, 158 cubic metres at 150, 16.5 tonnes at 1,500, and 625 square metres at 45 give 23,700, 24,750 and 28,125. The formwork, mostly labour, is the largest of the three, which is why it deserves the hardest look. Rates are local and move with the market; never carry a textbook rate into a real decision.

What the numbers are for

These quantities are not for designing the slab. Only the engineer's reinforcement schedule and drawings give real quantities. They are for sanity-checking a bid, comparing bids on a like-for-like basis, and asking better questions. A ratio that sits far outside the range of the other bids is a question, not an answer.

Measurement rules and the bill of quantities

Quantities are only comparable when everyone measures the same way. On larger work a cost consultant prepares a bill of quantities under a stated method of measurement, which defines what is measured net, what is measured gross, where waste is allowed and which items are deemed included. Without a shared method, one bidder measures formwork to the soffit only and another includes the edges, and their prices cannot be compared line by line. Where no formal bill exists, ask every bidder to state how he measured each main item; a single sentence often explains a gap that looked like a price difference.

Keep the takeoff alive during construction as well. When a change adds work, the quantity is measured against the same rules and priced at the agreed rate, which is why a clear measurement basis at tender makes changes faster and cheaper to settle.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is carrying a planning ratio or a textbook rate into a decision as though it were a measured number. A rule of thumb can tell you a bid looks odd; it cannot tell you what the building will cost. The second risk is a floor cycle assumption buried in the price: if it is optimistic, the overrun appears months later as time-related cost, long after the price was accepted.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner checks only the concrete, because it is easy and familiar, and accepts the formwork and the floor cycle without question. Another is using a textbook truck size or pump rate. Confirm actual local truck capacity and a realistic pump output with the supplier, because a pour plan built on the wrong numbers fails on the day.

How you will use it

For every major concrete element, do the volume yourself. Convert reinforcement to kilograms per square metre of floor and compare across bids. Ask every bidder for quantities as well as prices, and ask what floor cycle the price assumes, then what happens if it slips by one day. Treat every ratio as a planning check only. Professional sign-off required: structural engineer of record for reinforcement quantities; a cost consultant for rates.
checklist: Calculate the concrete volume of every major element yourself.
Convert reinforcement to kilograms per square metre of floor before comparing bids.
Ask every bidder for quantities, not just prices.
Ask what floor cycle the price assumes and what one extra day per floor costs.
Confirm real local truck capacity and pump rate with the supplier.
Treat every ratio and textbook rate as a planning check, never a design figure.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: Three bids for the same floor carry reinforcement of 26, 28 and 41 kilograms per square metre. The high bidder is also the cheapest overall. What do you do?
selftest.a: Ask the high bidder to show his reinforcement quantities and explain the difference, and ask the engineer of record which figure matches the design. A bidder carrying far more steel yet pricing lowest overall may have an error elsewhere, such as underpriced formwork or an optimistic floor cycle. Resolve the discrepancy before award, not after.

apply: Take any rectangular slab dimensions you choose and compute concrete volume with 5 percent waste, reinforcement at 100 kilograms per cubic metre plus 10 percent, kilograms per square metre, and formwork contact area.
sources: Takeoff methods follow standard estimating practice. Reinforcement ratios, waste allowances and productivity figures are planning rules of thumb that vary with system and market; confirm with the engineer of record and local suppliers. All figures are hypothetical.

title: The Programme, the Critical Path and the Price of a Week
summary: The master programme is the baseline, the critical path sets the finish date, and the rolling look-ahead is where the truth about progress appears. Preliminaries price the contractor's time on site, and the owner's own cost of delay is usually several times larger.
body:
Mr Shabazz, a building's finish date is set by one chain of activities, the critical path, and every week on site has a price for both the contractor and the owner. If you know both prices, you can make delay decisions as arithmetic rather than argument.

In plain English

The programme, or schedule, lists the activities, how long each takes and which must finish before others can start. Most activities can slip a little without moving the finish date; that slack is called float. One chain has no float. That chain is the critical path, and a day lost on it is a day lost at the end. The owner's job is to know which activities are on that chain and to watch them.

The critical path method

Each activity has a duration and logical links to its predecessors. Working forwards through the network gives each activity its earliest start and finish; working backwards from the end date gives its latest start and finish. Where earliest and latest are the same, there is no float, and the activity is critical. A good baseline programme is logic-linked, so that delaying one activity visibly pushes the ones that depend on it, and is updated monthly against actual progress.

The look-ahead and percent plan complete

The master programme is the baseline. The truth is in the rolling three-week look-ahead, where foremen commit to specific tasks for the coming week. A measure from Last Planner practice, percent plan complete, counts how many committed tasks were actually completed, and records the reason for every miss. It is an industry practice, not a standard. A falling percent plan complete, with the same reasons repeating (materials late, design information missing, area not ready), is an early warning weeks before the master programme turns red.

Preliminaries: the price of time

Preliminaries, also called general conditions and covered in MasterFormat Division 01, are the cost of running the site. They split into fixed costs (mobilisation, erecting and dismantling a crane, hoarding, demobilisation), time-related costs (supervision, crane hire, site accommodation, security, temporary power, dewatering running costs) and temporary works design and checking. The time-related part is the contractor's weekly price of being on site.

A worked example

Take a hypothetical network: activity A, 4 weeks; then B, 6 weeks, and C, 3 weeks, both after A; then D, 2 weeks, after both B and C.

  1. Path A, B, D is 4 plus 6 plus 2, which is 12 weeks. Path A, C, D is 4 plus 3 plus 2, which is 9 weeks. The longer path sets the finish: 12 weeks, and A, B and D are critical.
  2. C has 12 minus 9, which is 3 weeks of float. A two-week delay to C moves nothing; a two-week delay to B moves the finish by two weeks.
  3. Now price time. Suppose time-related preliminaries are 1,000,000 over a 50-week programme: 20,000 a week.
  4. The owner's own cost of delay is separate. Suppose construction interest of 15,000 a week and lost rent of 25,000 a week: 40,000 a week, before any extension fees on the loan.
  5. Run a sensitivity. At plus 4, 8 and 12 weeks, the contractor's prolongation is 80,000, 160,000 and 240,000; the owner's own loss is 160,000, 320,000 and 480,000. The combined price of a week is about 60,000.

With that number, a proposal to spend 50,000 to recover two weeks of critical-path delay is an easy yes, and the same spend on an activity with float is waste.

Negotiating the cost of time

Ask for the preliminaries breakdown before naming a preferred bidder, while you still have competition. Compare weekly rates between bidders, not totals, because a low total can hide a short programme. Agree the weekly rate in the contract as the measure of compensable prolongation, so that a delay claim is a multiplication rather than a dispute. Concede a fair rate and hold the definitions, and never let temporary works design be value-engineered out of the preliminaries. All figures here are illustrative; rates and percentages are commercial practice, not standards.

Owner's activities on the programme

The programme is not only the contractor's. Owner activities belong on it too: design information release dates, owner-supplied equipment, permit approvals, utility connections and the owner's own decisions on finishes. They are often the ones that drive delay claims, because a contractor cannot build what has not been designed or approved. Ask for them to be shown as logic-linked activities with dates, so a late owner item visibly pushes the work that depends on it.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a programme that looks green while the look-ahead is failing. A master programme can show on time for months while percent plan complete falls and the same reasons repeat; the delay is real long before it reaches the baseline.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner compares preliminaries as totals and picks the lowest, without asking whether the programme behind it is credible. A 900,000 total over 40 weeks is 22,500 a week, dearer per week than 1,000,000 over 50, and if the 40-week programme is fiction the owner pays for the extra weeks later.

How you will use it

Require a logic-linked baseline showing the critical path, updated monthly. Ask for the three-week look-ahead and percent plan complete, with reasons for misses, at every meeting. Know your weekly cost of delay and the contractor's weekly preliminaries rate, and use the combined figure to judge acceleration proposals. Professional sign-off required: a qualified scheduler for delay analysis, and construction counsel for prolongation clauses.
checklist: Require a logic-linked baseline programme that shows the critical path.
Ask which activities are critical and how much float the others carry.
Track the three-week look-ahead and percent plan complete with reasons for every miss.
Get the preliminaries breakdown before naming a preferred bidder.
Compare weekly preliminaries rates, not totals.
Know your own weekly cost of delay: interest, lost income and loan extension fees.
Agree the weekly rate in the contract as the measure of compensable prolongation.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: The master programme shows the job on time, but percent plan complete has fallen from 80 to 55 percent over four weeks, mostly with the reason 'design information not available'. What does it tell you, and what do you do?
selftest.a: It tells you the programme is about to slip and the cause sits with the owner's design team, so the delay may be yours to pay. Ask the design team for a list of outstanding information with dates, check which items feed critical-path activities, and get a recovery plan before the contractor files a time claim.

apply: Draw a four-activity network of your own, find the critical path and the float on the non-critical activity, then price a three-week delay to the critical path using a hypothetical weekly rate.
sources: Critical path method and float follow standard scheduling practice; percent plan complete comes from Last Planner System practice and is not a standard. Preliminaries are covered by CSI MasterFormat Division 01. All figures are hypothetical; rates are commercial practice.

title: The Site Logistics Plan and Fire Safety on an Unfinished Building
summary: Most slippage on a tight site comes from congestion, so a logistics plan drawn per phase finds the one constraint that sets the pace. A building under construction is also at its most combustible and least protected, and the codes put real duties on the owner.
body:
Mr Shabazz, on a tight site the gate, the crane or the turning space usually decides the pace, not the engineering. And the same building is never more vulnerable to fire than while it is being built, which the codes treat as the owner's problem as well as the contractor's.

In plain English

A site logistics plan is a set of drawings, one per phase, showing how materials, people and machines get on, move around and get off the site. It shows gates, the haul route, laydown areas, stockpiles, the crane or hoist and its swing radius, the pedestrian route, welfare facilities, and fire department access. Every site has a constraint, the single thing that limits throughput, and the constraint sets the pace of everything behind it. That is the theory of constraints applied to a building site.

Reading a logistics plan

Look first for the constraint. If trucks can only enter one at a time and must reverse in, the gate is the constraint. If one crane serves every trade, crane time is. Then check that the plan changes with the phases: the laydown area used during the frame may be where the ground-floor slab goes later. The areas nearest the gate are often finished last and seen first by everyone, including buyers and tenants, so their finishes need protecting.

The owner's obligations

Under Design-Build especially, the contractor owns his logistics: you observe and ask. But some items are the owner's and sit on the owner's critical path: access agreements with neighbours, crane oversail permissions, utility applications, street occupation permits, and any staging land outside the boundary. Track them as owner deliverables with dates.

Fire safety during construction

A building under construction has sprinklers not yet live, alarms not connected, rated walls and doors not installed, and formwork, packaging, fuel and hot work everywhere. In American practice three documents govern: IBC Chapter 33, Safeguards During Construction; IFC Chapter 33, Fire Safety During Construction and Demolition; and NFPA 241, with NFPA 51B for hot work. Recent editions place duties on the owner, including a written site safety plan and a designated responsible person [unverified — confirm independently]. Verify chapter numbers and requirements against the edition your jurisdiction has adopted.

Five requirements to remember: water before fuel, meaning a working water supply for firefighting before combustible material arrives in quantity; access before fuel, meaning a clear, all-weather route for fire apparatus; a standpipe that keeps pace with the building as it rises; at least one usable, lit stair; and controlled hot work with a permit and a fire watch that continues after the work stops, because smouldering material ignites later.

A March 2017 fire at a five-storey wood-framed apartment building under construction in Raleigh, North Carolina, as publicly reported, shows the pattern: maximum fuel, minimum protection. Read the public accounts before quoting detail.

A worked example

Suppose a hypothetical site has one gate, and each truck needs 20 minutes to enter, unload and leave.

  1. In an 8-hour delivery window, 480 minutes divided by 20 is 24 trucks a day.
  2. The excavation needs 340 truck loads of spoil removed. At 24 a day that is about 14 working days of haulage, and no faster machine changes it.
  3. If ready-mix trucks for a large pour need the same gate, the pour day and haulage cannot overlap. That is a sequencing decision, visible only on the logistics plan.
  4. Now fire access. Suppose the plan puts a laydown area across the fire apparatus route during the frame stage, before sprinklers are live. That is a code question, not a convenience question. Move the laydown or create an alternative route, and confirm it with the fire official in writing.
  5. Price the alternative: if a second gate costs 30,000 in hoarding and traffic management and halves the haulage duration to 7 days, compare it with 7 days at a combined weekly time cost of 60,000 a week, about 84,000 for seven working days. The second gate pays.

The neighbours and the street

The logistics plan also faces outward. Crane oversail across a neighbour's land usually needs that owner's written agreement. Hoarding on a public footway, a loading bay in the street and temporary traffic management need permits with conditions and fixed hours. Deliveries may be restricted to set times by a local authority. Each restriction shrinks the delivery window, and a shorter window means fewer trucks a day through the same constraint. Put the permitted hours into the truck arithmetic before you believe a haulage duration.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a construction fire. Beyond the danger to life, it means a builder's risk insurance claim, an investigation, possible stop-work orders and months of delay. The second risk is a logistics plan drawn once for the frame and never revised, so later phases fight for space the plan never gave them.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks of logistics as the contractor's housekeeping. It is a priced decision about the pace of the job, and where trucks queue becomes a cost. The other mistake is assuming fire safety is someone else's job until the building is finished.

How you will use it

Ask for a logistics plan per phase and identify its constraint. Track the owner's own permits and agreements as critical-path items. Ask to see the site fire safety plan, the named responsible person, the hot work permit system and the standpipe plan before combustible material arrives. Professional sign-off required: fire protection engineer and the local fire official; the contractor's competent safety professional.
checklist: Ask for a logistics plan per phase and identify its constraint.
Track access agreements, utility applications and permits as owner critical-path items.
Confirm water supply and fire apparatus access exist before combustible material arrives.
Check the standpipe rises with the building and one lit stair is usable.
Require a hot work permit system with a fire watch that continues after work stops.
Ask for the written site fire safety plan and the named responsible person.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: During the frame stage, before the sprinklers are live, you see a laydown area placed across the fire department access route. The superintendent says it is only temporary. What do you do?
selftest.a: Treat it as a code and life-safety issue, not a convenience. Ask that the route be cleared or an alternative approved, and confirm with the fire official in writing. Construction-phase fire rules in IBC and IFC Chapter 33 and NFPA 241 (verify against the adopted edition) exist precisely because the building is most combustible and least protected now.

apply: For any site you know, sketch the gate, haul route, laydown, crane and fire access, then name the single constraint you think would set the pace.
sources: IBC Chapter 33, IFC Chapter 33, NFPA 241 and NFPA 51B as commonly cited; owner duties and chapter numbering vary by edition [unverified — confirm independently]. Raleigh fire summarised from public reports. Truck arithmetic is hypothetical; percent plan complete and theory of constraints are practice, not standards.

title: Setting Out, Datum, and the Level Chain That Fixes Your Floor
summary: Every level on a project descends from a datum made physical by a benchmark, so a wrong benchmark makes every level wrong together. On flat ground, drainage falls and flood rules set a chain of levels that ends in the finished floor level and the earthworks budget.
body:
Mr Shabazz, every height on every drawing is measured from one reference point, and if two consultants use different ones, nothing fits and nobody finds out until something is built. On flat ground, a chain of levels starting at a drain you do not own decides your finished floor level and your fill budget.

In plain English

A datum is the reference surface that all elevations are measured from. It is made physical on site by a benchmark, a fixed point whose elevation is known. Setting out is the work of transferring the design's positions and levels onto the ground from those reference points. If the benchmark is wrong, or two consultants use different datums, every level is wrong together, and the error is discovered when a pipe will not connect or a floor meets a road at the wrong height.

What a survey must give you

Engage a licensed surveyor in the correct jurisdiction and obtain four things, ideally as separate titled deliverables. A boundary survey fixes where the site legally begins and ends. A topographic survey gives existing ground levels and features. A utility survey locates buried services. And a survey of the levels of everything you must connect to, such as the road edge, the public storm drain and the sewer invert, gives the fixed points your design must meet. Require permanent benchmarks installed on site, shown on the drawings with coordinates and elevations, and physically protected from plant, because a benchmark knocked by an excavator moves every level set from it.

The level chain

On flat ground, water needs a fall to drain, and fall consumes height. The chain starts at the discharge point, often a public drain you do not own, and works upward: the drain invert, plus the fall along your pipe, plus the pipe depth and cover, gives the lowest level your ground-floor drainage can leave the building at. Separately, the design flood level plus the required freeboard gives the lowest level a floor may sit at. Whichever is higher governs, and the difference between that and existing ground is fill you must import and compact.

Flood levels and freeboard are regulatory inputs. Obtain them in writing from the authority having jurisdiction, never verbally and never from a neighbour's project.

A worked example

Suppose a hypothetical site with existing ground at 11.50 metres above datum, and a building of 1,000 square metres.

  1. The public drain invert, confirmed by survey, is 10.00 metres.
  2. Your drain runs 100 metres at a 1 percent fall, so it rises 1.00 metre: the pipe's upstream invert is 11.00 metres.
  3. Pipe, bedding, cover and the slab above it add 1.20 metres: drainage requires a floor at no less than 12.20 metres.
  4. The authority's design flood level is 12.00 metres and the required freeboard is 0.50 metres: flood rules require a floor at no less than 12.50 metres.
  5. Flood governs at 12.50 metres. Raising the floor from existing ground of 11.50 needs about 1.00 metre of fill under the 1,000 square metre building: about 1,000 cubic metres compacted, before landscaping and ramps.
  6. Now suppose the record drawing showed the drain invert at 9.60, but the surveyor finds 10.00. Had the design relied on the record, the pipe would have arrived 0.40 metres too low to discharge. Buried-service records are frequently wrong; confirm by survey.

Setting out and checking it

Once design levels are fixed, the surveyor sets out gridlines and levels from the control points, and the contractor builds from them. Good practice is to check setting out independently at key stages: before excavation, before the first foundations, before the first suspended floor and before the envelope. A gridline that is out by 50 millimetres at foundation level becomes a column out of position on every floor above, and the cheapest moment to find it is before concrete is placed. Ask that each check be recorded with the date, the control point used and the result.

Keep the control network itself under review. Control points are often placed near the boundary to keep them out of the way, which is exactly where neighbours' work and deliveries disturb them. A short, routine check of each benchmark against the others at the start of each phase finds a disturbed point before anyone sets out from it.

Finally, keep the datum consistent across time as well as across consultants. A later extension, a utility connection or a lender's monitoring surveyor will need the same benchmark years from now, so the record drawings should state it clearly.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is two datums in one project. A civil engineer working to one benchmark and an architect to another can differ by tens of centimetres, and every drawing will look correct on its own. Insist every drawing from every consultant states its datum in the title block, and confirm only one is in use.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner tries to save earthworks money by trimming the freeboard. Freeboard is the margin between a floor and a flood; reducing it turns a cost into a flood risk that cannot be undone after the slab is cast. If the budget is tight, find savings where failure is a defect, not a flood.

How you will use it

Commission boundary, topographic and utility surveys as separate deliverables, plus the levels of everything you connect to. Require protected permanent benchmarks. Have your civil engineer walk you through the level chain from discharge point to finished floor level, so you see what drives your fill quantity. Get the flood level and freeboard in writing. Professional sign-off required: licensed land surveyor and civil engineer; the authority having jurisdiction for flood levels.
checklist: Engage a licensed surveyor and get boundary, topographic and utility surveys as separate deliverables.
Require permanent benchmarks on site, recorded on the drawings and protected from plant.
Make every consultant state the datum in the title block and confirm only one is used.
Obtain the design flood level and required freeboard in writing from the authority.
Confirm the drainage discharge invert by survey, not from a record drawing.
Have the civil engineer walk you through the level chain to finished floor level.
Never reduce freeboard to save earthworks cost.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: The architect's ground-floor level is 0.30 metres higher than the civil engineer's drawing for the same slab. Both say their drawing is correct. What is the most likely cause, and what do you do?
selftest.a: The most likely cause is two different datums or benchmarks. Ask each consultant to state the datum and benchmark they used, have the surveyor confirm the correct one on site, and require every drawing to carry the datum in its title block. Then recheck the level chain against the one agreed datum.

apply: Using hypothetical numbers of your own, work a level chain from a drain invert through pipe fall and cover to a floor level, then compare it with a flood level plus freeboard and compute the fill volume.
sources: Survey and datum practice follow standard surveying and civil engineering practice. Flood levels and freeboard requirements are set by the authority having jurisdiction and, in American practice, by IBC and ASCE 24 as adopted; confirm locally. All figures are hypothetical.

title: Week Two Review: Quantities, Time, Logistics and Levels
summary: Six scenario questions on quantity takeoff, the critical path and the price of time, site logistics and construction fire safety, and the level chain. The week's thread is that the numbers behind a price and a date can be checked by the owner.
body:
Mr Shabazz, this week turned drawings into quantities, a programme into a price per week, and a survey into a floor level. Work each question before reading the answer, and say the arithmetic aloud.

Question 1. A floor measures 30 by 20 metres. One bidder carries 16.5 tonnes of reinforcement, another 24 tonnes. How do you compare them, and what do you ask?

Answer. Normalise to the floor area of 600 square metres: 16,500 divided by 600 is 27.5 kilograms per square metre, and 24,000 divided by 600 is 40. The gap is large enough to be a question. Ask both bidders for their quantities, and ask the engineer of record which figure matches the design. Ratios are for sanity checks, not design, so the engineer's schedule settles it.

Question 2. Activities: A 5 weeks; B 7 weeks after A; C 4 weeks after A; D 3 weeks after B and C. What is the finish, which path is critical, and how much float does C have?

Answer. Path A, B, D is 5 plus 7 plus 3, which is 15 weeks. Path A, C, D is 5 plus 4 plus 3, which is 12 weeks. The finish is 15 weeks, A, B and D are critical, and C has 3 weeks of float. A two-week slip in C costs nothing; a two-week slip in B costs two weeks at the end.

Question 3. Bidder one prices time-related preliminaries at 1,000,000 over 50 weeks. Bidder two prices 900,000 over 40 weeks. Which is cheaper?

Answer. Per week, bidder one is 20,000 and bidder two 22,500. Bidder two is cheaper in total only if his 40-week programme is credible. If the job really takes 50 weeks, his time cost reaches about 1,125,000 at his own rate, and the owner also carries ten weeks of his own delay cost. Ask what was excluded and test the programme before comparing totals.

Question 4. The master programme is green, but percent plan complete has fallen for four weeks with the same reason recorded each time: materials not on site. What is happening?

Answer. The programme is about to slip, and procurement is the cause. A falling percent plan complete with a repeating reason is an early warning that arrives weeks before the baseline shows it. Check the long-lead log and the delivery dates, and ask for a recovery plan now.

Question 5. Before sprinklers are live, a laydown area blocks the fire department access route. What governs, and what do you do?

Answer. Construction-phase fire safety rules govern: in American practice IBC and IFC Chapter 33 and NFPA 241, to be verified against the adopted edition. Access before fuel is one of the core requirements. Have the route cleared or an alternative approved and confirmed with the fire official in writing, and check the site fire safety plan names a responsible person.

Question 6. Drainage requires a floor at 12.10 metres, and the flood level plus freeboard requires 12.40 metres. Existing ground is 11.60 metres under a 1,200 square metre building. What is the floor level and roughly how much fill?

Answer. The higher requirement governs, so 12.40 metres. Fill is 12.40 minus 11.60, which is 0.80 metres, times 1,200 square metres: about 960 cubic metres compacted under the building, before ramps and landscaping. Do not reduce freeboard to cut it.

Recap

A takeoff turns drawings into quantities you can check. Concrete is volume plus waste; reinforcement is estimated from a ratio and compared as kilograms per square metre; formwork is contact area and carries the labour that sets the floor cycle. Confirm truck sizes and pump rates with the supplier.

The critical path sets the finish date, and float is the slack on everything else. The look-ahead and percent plan complete are where progress truth appears first. Preliminaries price the contractor's time; the owner's own cost of delay is usually larger. Know both weekly numbers and use them to judge acceleration.

The logistics plan finds the constraint, usually the gate, the crane or the turning space. The owner's own permits and agreements are critical-path items. Construction is the most dangerous fire period in a building's life: water and access before fuel, a rising standpipe, a usable stair, and controlled hot work with a continuing fire watch.

Every level descends from one datum and one benchmark. The level chain runs from a discharge point you do not own to your finished floor, and the flood level plus freeboard often governs. Confirm inverts by survey and keep the freeboard.

The thread: the numbers behind a price and a date are checkable by the owner in minutes, and checking them is how the owner earns the right to ask better questions. Professional sign-off required: the engineer of record for quantities, a scheduler for delay analysis, a fire protection engineer and the fire official for construction fire safety, and a licensed surveyor for datum and levels.

Notice that each of these lessons ends in the same move: convert an assumption into a number, then ask who is carrying the number if it is wrong. A reinforcement ratio, a floor cycle, a weekly rate, a truck interval and a drain invert are all assumptions until somebody measures them. The owner does not need to measure them himself; he needs to know which ones have been measured, by whom, and which are still guesses.

Next week goes below the surface, into the ground investigation that every one of these numbers ultimately depends on.
checklist: Normalise reinforcement to kilograms per square metre before comparing bids.
Identify the critical path and the float in any programme you are shown.
Compare preliminaries per week and test the programme behind them.
Read a falling percent plan complete as an early warning.
Keep fire access and water supply ahead of combustible material on site.
Confirm the governing floor level from both drainage and flood requirements.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: What single weekly number would you calculate first before judging any proposal to accelerate the programme?
selftest.a: The combined weekly cost of time: the contractor's time-related preliminaries per week plus the owner's own weekly cost of delay, such as interest and lost income. With it, acceleration spending on critical-path activities can be judged as arithmetic.
